#6739. Dutch Apple Pie

Dutch apple pie is the upgrade the fall classic needs. With a nutty, streusel topping, this cozy dessert will have you coming back for slice after slice. It’s also easier to make than the traditional version because there’s no need to cook the apple filling ahead of time. In fact, some of us will be swapping out our traditional apple pie recipe for this one for Thanksgiving this year.

Lightly flour your work surface, then roll out the chilled dough into a 12-inch circle. Carefully move it to a 9-inch pie dish. Gently lift the edges and let the dough settle into the pan. Make sure not to stretch the dough. Press it firmly into the bottom and sides. Pop it in the fridge until it’s cold (about 30 minutes), or freeze it for 10 minutes if you’re in a hurry.

Grab a medium bowl and whisk together the granulated sugar, flour, cinnamon, and salt.

In a large bowl, whisk together the egg, sour cream, and vanilla. Add the dry ingredients and whisk until the mixture is nice and smooth.

Move a rack to the center of your oven and preheat it to 350°. In a medium bowl, whisk together the brown sugar, flour, granulated sugar, walnuts, oats, and cinnamon. Add the butter and use a fork or pastry cutter to work it in until crumbly.

Spread the apples evenly in your prepared pie crust. Pour the filling over the apples, then sprinkle the crumble topping all over.

Bake the pie until the crust and crumble are golden brown and you don’t see any more moisture. This should take about an hour. Once it’s done, let the pie cool on a wire rack until it reaches room temperature, then pop it in the fridge for an hour before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Because this pie has a sour cream and egg-based filling, store leftovers covered in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6738. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. #6737. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6736. With the ‘New’ Yeezy, Ye Says He Wants to ‘Let the Clothes Do the Talking.’ But Who’s Listening?

“I don’t have a lot of words tonight,” Ye told me, not long after concluding his Yeezy Season 01 runway show in Los Angeles on Wednesday evening. “I’ll let the clothes do the talking.”

You might read that quote and be surprised to hear that Ye said it warmly, with an all-32-bared smile. But for those still paying attention, his relatively upbeat demeanor tracks with the tame-not-turnt persona that Ye has performed through most of 2026; the one that’s been slowly-but-surely trying to reamass the cultural capital he’s spent most of the last decade either annihilating or reclaiming. Legions of fans have proven they’re still all in; the culture at large remains justifiably dubious. The question this week is, how will Ye’s return to fashion affect the calculus?

Upon arrival, a typical Hollywood warehouse exterior turned into a Frank Herbert-esque interior as soon as you crossed the threshold. Inside, a hundred or so guests sat on two rows of unbroken benches that encircled a large white mound in the center, lit by a heavenly white glow from above. Inside was a mix of the usual cool kids: models (including the runway-favorite teen rapper Nettspend) and recurring characters in the overarching, enduring Kanye Universe. There was Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo, who made conversation with Don C, while 2 Chainz was patiently posted up in a hooded black leather coat like ’98 Wesley Snipes. Big Sean, rebuffing the sweltering indoor temperatures in a shearling jacket over a crewneck sweater, caught up with Hit-Boy.

Models on the Yeezy Season 01 runway, which featured a characteristically minimalist set piece.

The 19-year-old rapper Nettspend walked in the show.

Once everyone was seated, the lights dimmed as the unmistakable opening piano note of “Runaway” set the show into motion, with one lone model striding out in a killer black trench. From there, two more models, men this time, walked out in the opposite direction; what followed was a bit of organized chaos with the number of models and paths alternating at random intervals to the tune of a playlist that zipped between new Ye music (UK garage vibes, it would seem) and a gothic orchestra not unlike the scores Danny Elfman used to chef up for Tim Burton.

The fits were crisp, practical and tactical. Most of the menswear was ready-made for basic maneuvers, while the women’s looks were sleek and casual, with a few Milla Jovovich-in-Fifth-Element skimpy ensembles thrown in because Ye can only restrain himself but so much. The most notable thing, about the guys especially, were the relatively streamlined silhouettes: close-cropped coats, bombers and vests, fitted pants and sweats. Where past Ye lines championed and emblazoned the path for the baggy wave, with oversized boots and pants you could swim in, Ye seemed to be brazenly planting a flag back on the opposite end of the spectrum.

Nearly 12 years, and a dozen lifetimes, since his debut Yeezy Season 1 runway show in 2015, the notion of a “Season 01”—his first formal showing since his damning 2022 show in Paris, the one with the “White Lives Matter” shirts—is a conspicuous attempt to clear the slate. All of his previous shows had been produced in collaboration with Adidas, who severed ties with Ye four years ago, after he tweeted a tirade of antisemetic remarks. This time around, to let the clothes tell it, Ye is locked in. I don’t have an image of every single Yeezy Season line seared into my brain, but I feel comfortable saying Ye’s latest was the first time I looked at one of his collections and objectively thought, I could wear that. Most of the gear is quite solid—and familiar Ye's running the same playbook with Season 01 that he’s run with his music, and to some degree, his persona. It’s the Yeezy gear you know and love(d), refined to make it that much more palatable, similar to the way a song like “Whatever Works” puts him back over chipmunk’d soul samples. And true to the title, it does indeed; the fact that it does is maybe a testament to the brilliance that got lost in the insanity. But is playing the hits (quite literally, with “Runaway” opening the show) what we want from one of the most paradigm-shifting—and absolutely chaotic—creative minds of our time?

Historically, Ye’s designs are so focused on an idea of utilitarianism that they ultimately come off as a bit drab, if not downright dystopian. Essentials like hoodies and beefy leather jackets are still central to his vision, but as the models strode around in his usual earth-toned palette—save for a handful of black looks to start, and a bright pop of reds at the end—it became clear that Ye was putting on the same show in a different kind of stadium. The same sci-fi silhouettes, tweaked to their cleanest shape and most pleasing hue, sans screenprinted hate speech. Ideologically, the runway show wasn’t far off from the experience of hearing his 2007 hit “Good Life” all these years later, ringing off stadium speakers, carrying 80,000 people along on a wave of wistfulness— even if Ye himself only performed approximately 75% of the lyrics against a backing track.

In keeping with all of his other moves this year, Yeezy Season 01 is Ye presenting a safer, rule-abiding version of himself: Ye with just art, no antics. Much in the way that his latest album, Bully, eschewed any lyrics that say, shouted out R. Kelly or Bill Cosby (which is more than can be said about 2024’s Vultures 1), it felt like a deep sigh of relief to see him present clothes that don’t feature appalling slogans, at a fashion show with Candace Owens nowhere in sight. But the compromise for a sanitized Kanye is also one that can’t help but feel anodyne as well. The New Ye doesn’t needle, but he’s lost Old Ye’s knack for trying something new. Of course, we’re also well over a decade into the Yeezy experiment—at this point, the present has caught up to the futuristic vision Ye first dreamt up back in 2015. There’s a whole new generation of aspiring designers creating in his image, kids who fancy themselves trailblazers whose paths just loop back to Ye: streamer Kai Cenat just launched his own clothing brand, Vivet, while N3on attended Wednesday night’s show, skipping the Yeezy space gleefully documenting every interaction. It feels as though all of this has happened before, and all of it will happen again.

Mystery. Intrigue. Chaos. This is the typical life cycle for a Ye project, be it music, fashion, or otherwise. An announcement materializes, hype ensues. Then, inevitably, the seams start to show and it becomes apparent that he isn’t inviting you on a pre-planned journey so much as building the plane in real time, seconds before takeoff. And then, through sheer force of will, or maybe even genius, the result ends up so captivating that the speedbumps hardly matter. He’s still a master showman, and all it takes is a strong yearning for the Old Ye to find yourself surrendering to it. The efficacy of that last factor, though, has undeniably waned over the years. For much of the 2020s, in the midst of many a manic outburst or worse, Ye’s messes have hardly cohered into something objectively beautiful. The intrigue curdled into perverse bemusement; for every unwavering diehard fan, there was a rubbernecker tapped in to watch the circus.

The 2026 version of Ye has been an exercise in proving how many people will show up when he shuts up, and whether he can make it back from the brink if he delivers the right spectacle.

The result is the most well-oiled the Yeezy Machine has ever been. An album that more or less dropped when he said it would, for once. A smattering of live shows across the world, each in a sold-out stadium boasting record-breaking rap concert attendance where he leans on his most enduring strengths: visual spectacle and a bulletproof catalog. The only area left to renegotiate is fashion…which brings us back to Wednesday night in LA.

These are the scenes you’d expect at a Ye event, but the first sign that the overall vibe was different and more relaxed was that the man himself was at the door, tucked off into a hallway, immaculately dressed in a fitted all-black leather fit offset by a ridiculously large and ornate gold waist fixture—every bit the Dune-caliber fit as the space we were standing in required. Ahead of the show, he posed backstage flanked by his wife, Bianca Censori, and the four kids he shares with his ex, Kim Kardashian (including 13-year-old North, who was sporting her unmistakable blue-raspberry locks). At Yeezy events past, you’d expect to see harried staff scrambling, while Ye was somewhere out of sight but exuding stress and anxiety out into the atmosphere. But on Wednesday, the 49-year-old beamed as friends made their way past him to their seats. Even a three-piece-suited Kid Cudi came over to say hello.

Ye backstage with his children, from left: North, Psalm, Chicago, and Saint West.

Fifteen years ago, Yeezy Season 01 would’ve caused a massive sea change in the menswear world almost instantaneously, with the wave starting in SoHo then slowly emanating out into the beyond. In 2026, does Kanye still move that needle? The Year in Ye has been one big display of his ability to Don Draper the culture at large, and shock us all by “how much it never happened.” There’s no controversy big enough to keep him away for too long and very few fences he can’t mend.

For example, Sean and Cudi ceased their umpteenth falling out with their old label boss two months ago at a guest-packed, blockbuster homecoming show in Chicago on Ye’s tour stop; their show of support tonight only underlined how deeply the hatchet has been buried yet again. When I spoke to Big Sean after the show, he could only marvel at how much Ye has “given” to the culture across all different categories. One-time GOOD Music COO Steven Victor said the show made him feel like Ye “has his shit together,” noting that Ye admitted to him that he was still working out the model patterns hours before showtime. In past Yeezy Seasons, the cram-effect would’ve been apparent, but here, Victor said he wouldn’t have noticed because it all seemed to go off so effortlessly.

As for the man himself? I spoke to him, but again, he didn’t have much to say, at least on the record. He seemed excited that I picked up on the intentional disharmony of the model routes, and explained that the space we were standing in was a “language I’ve been working on for 10 years” called “DROAM,” which refers to the minimalist design he hopes to apply to stores, urban planning, and a home for himself.

“I got a quote for you,” Victor interjected. “The king returns!” Ye laughed. The question remains, though: Is he welcome?

#6735. I Took Olive Oil Shots Every Morning For A Month—Is The Health Hype Real?

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

I’ll try just about anything that promises to make me look and feel better, but drinking olive oil? That one gave me pause—until I read up on the impressive benefits and found out Hailey Bieber does it every day. Suddenly, I was down to ditch my green juice habit to sip this alleged liquid gold.

But is there any real advantage to drinking it straight versus incorporating it into your regular diet? Or is it just another TikTok fad that sounds better on your FYP than it works IRL? I decided to take pre-made olive oil shots for an entire month to put the hype to the test. Here’s what happened.

If you didn’t already know, extra-virgin olive oil is a nutritional powerhouse! It’s rich in monounsaturated fats and antioxidants, and research has linked consumption to lower LDL (aka the “bad” cholesterol), better cardiovascular health, and reduced inflammation. It may also support healthy blood sugar levels and brain health, which is pretty cool considering it’s an ingredient we all probably have in our kitchen cabinets.

“Olive oil also contains polyphenols, which are natural plant compounds that help protect our cells from oxidative stress and support a healthy inflammatory response,” Maura MacDonald, M.S., R.D., C.S.S.D., registered dietitian at Thorne, tells Delish. “These compounds can benefit gut health too by interacting with the bacteria in our digestive system and helping to support microbial diversity and a healthy gut microbiome. It’s one of the reasons olive oil is such a staple of the Mediterranean diet, which has long been associated with better overall health and longevity.”

Listen, I knew that chugging olive oil wasn’t going to be a pleasant experience, but I wasn’t expecting it to be quite so, ahem, interesting. My main gripe was with the consistency: It was just a little too thick and viscous to go down easily, and every shot required a full pep talk.

I didn’t notice much difference after day 5, which left me feeling discouraged. I had hoped for an immediate click—glowing skin, boosted energy levels, less bloating, something!—but the only tangible evidence of my participation in the experiment was a glue-like coating that clung to my tonsils after every morning shot.

By week two, I called an audible and started adding lemon juice to the olive oil. Anything to cut the oiliness just a little—plus, the citrus brings its own nutritional perks! And while it wasn’t a perfect fix, it made the process a little more bearable.

Midway through the month, I started to notice improvements. My skin seemed more hydrated, my digestion was more regular, and I wasn’t dealing with the same post-meal bloating I’ve dealt with for years. I also found myself filling up faster, and I didn’t feel the same pull to go back for seconds. Whether it was the olive oil or a placebo effect, I’m not entirely sure, but at least I finally felt like the morning routine was doing something.

As the experiment progressed, I noticed my energy levels improve. I wasn’t exactly jumping out of bed like a morning person (let’s not get carried away here), but I was able to avoid the usual afternoon slump. I had fewer cravings too and wasn’t automatically reaching for snacks between mealtimes. My body just felt like it was functioning better.

I’m so glad you asked! Yes, yes, it does. According to MacDonald, it actually makes a big difference.

“Extra-virgin olive oil is generally the best choice for maximizing health benefits because it’s cold-pressed and unrefined, meaning it retains more of its natural antioxidants and polyphenols,” she explains. “This is the one you’re likely eating at a restaurant when they serve the bread.”

Regular virgin olive oil is also cold-pressed and offers similar benefits, but it has a slightly higher acidity level and milder flavor, while refined olive oil goes through additional processing that reduces even more of those benefits.

“I'd recommend reaching for extra-virgin olive oil whenever possible, especially formaking salad dressings, drizzling over vegetables, or adding to meals,” MacDonald adds. “It's an easy way to get the most nutritional value out of the olive oil you're already using.”

While, for the sake of the experiment, I drank it straight, MacDonald says that it’s actually not the most practical way to consume it.

“I'd recommend incorporating extra-virgin olive oil into your everyday meals instead,” she says. “Not only is it easier on digestion, but it can also help your body absorb fat-soluble vitamins from other foods.”

She doesn’t have to tell me twice. I’ll drizzle it on salads and roasted veggies, mix it with lemon (but for a dressing this time!), and add it to fish and whole grains.

“Using olive oil, a source of fat containing both mono- and polyunsaturated fats, in place of saturated fats like butter is another easy way to support heart health,” MacDonald continues. “It's really about making olive oil part of a balanced eating pattern, rather than treating it as something you need to incorporate each morning separately.”

While it’s not a downside per se, MacDonald points out that a typical serving of olive oil (a.k.a. one tablespoon) has about 120 calories and 14 grams of fat, so a two-tablespoon shot would total about 240 calories and 28 grams of fat. The TL;DR? While it’s a great source of heart-healthy monounsaturated fats and antioxidants, it’s also calorie-dense.

“Taking a shot every morning can add up quickly, especially if you're adding it on top of your usual diet—which may already include using olive oil or other fats in your meals and cooking processes,” she says. “Rather than thinking of olive oil as something extra you need to consume, I’d recommend using it in place of saturated fats, like butter or coconut oil, when applicable, as part of your everyday meals.”

I did notice changes in how I felt overall after taking olive oil shots every day, especially with my digestion. But given MacDonald’s advice that you can reap the same benefits from simply incorporating it into your everyday diet, I think I’ll retire the morning shots in favor of something I’ll actually enjoy—like O.O. on a salad or with a fresh piece of sourdough. I’ll get my daily dose the old-fashioned way, and reserve the shot glasses for my Friday nights.

#6734. A Close Look At the 10 Key Autumn/Winter 2026 Bag Trends

Compared with the wave of house debuts for spring/summer, the fall/winter 2026 season was business as usual—sort of. Only a handful of inaugural showcases this time around, but the sophomore collections brought plenty of ideas to the fore, including an abundance of ready-to-wear and bag trends.

Pieter Mulier focused on the former in his last show for Alaïa after a five-year stint, which Vogue’s Sarah Mower described as “quiet perfectionism”. “It’s just really clothes for real people, not for an image,” Mulier said. “To reduce, reduce. No bags, no jewelry. Only beauty and clothes and a naked shoe. Because that’s what Azzedine was.”

Yet, during his tenure, Mulier delivered a number of It-bags, the most recent being his Le Teckel—meaning “sausage dog” in French, for its slimline shape—which will hold its value far beyond his departure. In fact, he could be credited with influencing the current streamlined, top-handle bag trend —the east-west—designed with the same tuck-under-your-arm spirit as the Le Teckel—which was present across recent runway shows.

Top handles in various iterations, including this popular east-west shape, acted as props for the 15 models cast at Prada, each of whom wore four layered looks that transformed as they walked the runway. Elsewhere, the intentionally undone Amazona 18 bag, introduced at Loewe by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, returned in a swathe of new colorways and finishes.

Chanel also went bold with bags this season, exhibiting everything from supersized shoulder bags and siren-red croc-embossed companions to delicately embroidered flap bags. The mood Anthony Vaccarello conveyed at Saint Laurent, however, was quite the opposite: skinny envelopes clasped by models on his carpeted runway. These clutch wallets accompanied Vaccarello’s step-and-repeat of suits that comprised the opening eight looks–a nod to the 60th anniversary of the Le Smoking, one of the house’s most revolutionary contributions to the industry.

Along with clutches, minaudières were also a prominent trend this season; these jewel-like purses—akin to special occasion jewelry—had a strong presence at Loewe, Dior, and Chanel. The newcomer this season was the U-Shape bag (also known as the half moon bag), seen at Stella McCartney, Louis Vuitton, Polo Ralph Lauren, and Tod’s; think of it as the new slouch bag. This season, croc-embossing also appeared across an array of accessories, especially in bags. For all upcoming holiday festivities, tassel bags feel like an elegant touch to add to any ensemble. While textured bags complement any cozy outfit.

Here, Vogue brings you seven standout trends from the collections that are worth shopping right now.

The east-to-west silhouette from season’s past is more prominent than ever. From Chanel’s punchy color to Bottega Veneta's more neutral options, the elongated silhouette shows up in top handles, shoulders, and tote bags. Then there is Fendi’s iconic baguette bag, the gift that keeps on giving. Sleek yet spacious, it packs a punch without overdoing it.

This season—from Saint Laurent shoulder bags to Prada’s pouch bags—animal print bags are taking charge in every silhouette. Leopard, cheetah, zebra, and fawn spots are key this fall and winter. An animal print bag can add that personality to any outfit; think of it as a neutral.

Crocodile, whether real exotic leather or embossed, made its mark this season, too, elevating the simplest of shapes with a tactile, high-gloss finish. Prada, Celine, Chanel, and Tory Burch all made a case for croco. Lean into the trend by adding a neutral or bold color to your wardrobe; this texture adds that ultimate touch of luxury.

Tassels were once used to adorn a home, bringing a bit of elegance and opulence. This season, with the resurgence of Art Deco glamour, designers have been inspired to incorporate them into modern-day dressing, as seen at Bottega Veneta, Lanvin, and Ulla Johnson. Lean into the trend with a tassel bag that makes for event dressing.

Top-handle bags bring an entirely different vibe to the act of carrying a bag, since they can only be grasped with one hand or slipped into the crook of an arm. No bother: you’ll want the profiles of the new bags from Hermès, Dior and Prada on full display. More rigid top-handles leaned into doctor bag territory with curved proportions (see Miu Miu, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler), while others, such as Jonathan Anderson’s playful Cigale, offered a new everyday silhouette, fitting for night and day. This is the perfect bag to take from the office to an evening out, the ultimate investment for any wardrobe.

Winter is around the corner, and it's the perfect time to start building your cold-weather wardrobe. Pair a plush shearling bag (either lined or full-on plush); these bags are meant to complement your winter-cozy-yet-chic look. Available in an array of silhouettes, from pouch bags to tote bags, they are meant to complement any look, as seen at Simone Rocha, Bottega Veneta, and Fendi.

Shoulder bags are traditionally quite small, holding just a few belongings, but the shows offered a fresh crop of styles scaled up ever so slightly. They still fit snugly on the shoulder, tucking easily under the arm, with more room for everyday items–some (from the likes of Chanel, Miu Miu and Bottega Veneta) could even hold a laptop.

Consider the crescent bag the slouchy bag’s more sculptural cousin—still slouchy but not expressly relaxed. This season, the curved half moon (or U shape) silhouette was spotted everywhere from Dior to Tod’s, Polo, Stella, and Louis Vuitton. Choose from bigger sizes for day, or a smaller one for the evening. Think of this as the new slouch bag of the season.

Evening affairs—be they a wedding or a gala—call for accents that are a conversation starter. Designers interpreted the assignment differently, but many brought whimsy to it: Chanel strung a glossy pomegranate from a wristlet chain, while Dior turned the frog prince into a valiant dinner companion. From metal-finished to leather minaudieres, these bags are exquisite, almost like a jewelry piece that holds just the essentials.

Once upon a time, clutches were restricted to evening use, but recent seasons have changed that mindset. Look to the supple, pillowy pouches at Loewe, Bottega Veneta, and Stella McCartney, which would be just as fitting out on the town as they would on your morning commute. The clutch has proven to be a fashion favorite, especially this season; we have seen it worn during fashion week.

#6733. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6730. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie

This pumpkin pie recipe has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics. It’s the kind of Thanksgiving dessert readers return to year after year—and not just on the holiday. The filling is silky and rich, deftly spiced with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves, and tastes unmistakably of pumpkin.

Sweetened condensed milk and a splash of heavy cream give the custard its velvety texture, while maple syrup and vanilla add depth. We use canned pumpkin purée (Libby’s is our pick) for its consistent texture and concentrated flavor. A blind-baked crust, finished with an egg wash, keeps things crisp underneath all that creamy filling.

The trickiest part is knowing when to stop baking. Look for slightly puffed, set edges and a center that still jiggles gently, like Jell-O. The filling will firm up as the pie cools, giving you smooth, custardy slices. Serve with a generous dollop of whipped cream.

Make it the finale in a classic Thanksgiving feast →

Sure. We tested this very filling in several store-bought pie crusts, with good results. Use an unbaked 9" pie shell and blind-bake it according to the package instructions before adding the filling. Packaged crusts may bake faster than homemade dough, so don’t automatically follow the crust-baking times in this recipe.

Yes. This recipe calls for 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée. A standard 15-oz. can contains about 1¾ cups, so you’ll need to open a second can. Save the leftovers for another of our favorite pumpkin purée recipes. And be sure you’re buying plain pumpkin purée, not canned pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices.

Bake the pie up to a day ahead, let it cool completely, then wrap and refrigerate until you’re ready to serve. For longer-term planning, you can freeze the baked pie for up to 3 months.

2 hours (plus 4 hours 30 minutes for chilling)

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie dish. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lightly beat 1 large egg, room temperature, in a small bowl just to blend, then brush over inside of crust (not the crimped edges) and continue to bake until crust is set and beginning to lightly brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 325°. Lightly beat 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, and remaining 2 large eggs, room temperature, in a clean small bowl just to blend. Whisk ⅓ cup (67 g) sugar, 1 tsp. ground cinnamon, ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ½ tsp. ground ginger, ¼ tsp. ground cloves, and ¼ tsp. ground nutmeg in a large bowl until no clumps remain. Add egg mixture, 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée, ⅔ cup sweetened condensed milk, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. maple syrup, and 2 tsp. vanilla extract and whisk until smooth. Pour into cooled crust. Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 60–75 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with whipped cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature. You can also freeze pumpkin pie up to 3 months in advance.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in November 2016; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving pies →

#6729. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6728. Crock-Pot Chicken Noodle Soup

The pinnacle of cozy, comforting food is chicken noodle soup. When you need something warming and satisfying, there’s just nothing better. While our classic recipe is already easy to whip up, tossing all of your ingredients in the slow cooker makes this soup easier than ever. After a few hours and very little effort, you’ll have the coziest meal on your hands, ready to warm you up all fall and winter long.

What People Are Saying:“Perfect for snow days. Easy to make and there is no wrong time for soup” - evabnyc2372

“ Very easy....very good thank god I made a big pot bc I have 3 boys my oldest had 5 servings and my youngest had two giant servings my middle son had 3” - ashleybaby3586

The best thing about this recipe? It’s not necessary to cook the chicken before putting it in the soup—let your slow cooker do all the hard work for you. Place the boneless, skinless chicken breasts in the slow cooker, along with the veggies, herbs, butter, and broth. Season with salt and pepper, then cook on high with the lid closed for 2 1/2 hours.

By now, the chicken should be cooked and tender. Transfer it to a plate, and after letting it cool slightly, use 2 forks to shred it (or whatever is your favorite shredding method).

Discard the thyme, rosemary, and bay leaf from the slow cooker, then add the shredded chicken back in along with the egg noodles. Cover and cook on High for about 5 to 10 minutes—you're looking for the noodles to be al dente.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have leftovers, I strongly suggest that you store the noodles separately from the broth. If they’re stored together, the noodles will soak up the liquid and turn to mush, and there won’t be any broth left. If you’d like to cook this soup in advance, the same recommendation applies, though if you’re making it ahead of time, I'd recommend skipping the noodles completely. You can add them to the broth when you reheat the soup, and they should be fully cooked in just 5 minutes.

Same deal if you're freezing—the soup itself freezes well and can be reheated whenever the craving hits, but the noodles will get mushy sitting in all of that broth, so I'd recommend cooking them off fresh!

#6727. How to Moisturize Your Scalp in 6 Easy Steps

Whenever my scalp feels tight and itchy and I notice white flakes falling, I wonder whether my love of hot showers (yes, I’m guilty of turning my small NYC shower into the equivalent of a hot spring) or my daily use of hot styling tools might be contributing. Whatever the cause, I know it’s time to give my scalp some extra attention.

As Hadley King, MD, a New York City board-certified dermatologist, explains, dry skin is generally characterized by water loss and a disrupted skin barrier. The same applies to the scalp, which Dr. King says needs both water-binding ingredients and barrier-supporting lipids to stay moisturized.

Several things can cause a dry scalp. Morgan Rabach, MD, a board-certified dermatologist and cofounder of LM Medical NYC, lists overwashing, using hot water in the shower, excessive hot tool use, and overprocessing hair with harsh chemicals as habits that may contribute. Certain skin conditions, like eczema or seborrheic dermatitis, and environmental factors such as cold weather or low humidity are also common causes.

Additionally, Y. Claire Chang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm, adds that sebum production can decrease with age and during hormonal changes, making your scalp even more prone to dryness. These are all things you’ll want to address because, as we know, healthy hair comes from a healthy scalp. “The scalp is an extension of the skin on the face and body,” says Dr. Chang. “It is important to maintain a healthy skin barrier on the scalp just like the rest of the body.”

Luckily, it’s not too hard to keep your scalp moisturized. Just consider adding the following steps to your routine.

The first step to moisturizing your scalp is washing it with a gentle shampoo formulated with hydrating ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid. Dr. King agrees and recommends using a gentle, non-medicated shampoo rather than a harsher clarifying shampoo if the scalp is dry. “The goal is to remove sweat, sebum, and product buildup without stripping the scalp’s protective lipids,” she says.

She says to look for gentle surfactants and recommends a shampoo like the Nutrire S.1 Calm Shampoo for Dry Scalp, which contains humectants like glycerin and panthenol to retain water and watermelon seed oil to provide emollient lipids that smooth dry skin. Alexis Stephens, DO, a board-certified dermatologist based in Coral Springs, Florida, likes the Vanicream Shampoo for Sensitive Skin as it is made without several of the most common irritants found in products, such as fragrance and essential oils. “It’s a good option for people with sensitive scalps or those who experience irritation from fragranced hair products,” Dr. Stephens says. “While it isn’t a moisturizer itself, it helps establish a gentler cleansing routine that supports scalp comfort.”

Like your face, your scalp skin can get dry when you overdo exfoliation. “A dry scalp generally doesn’t need aggressive scrubbing,” Dr. King says. “If someone has significant scale, it’s important to determine whether we’re dealing with seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis rather than simply trying to exfoliate it away.”

After shampooing, Dr. Chang recommends using a moisturizing scalp treatment. Look for nourishing ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, or panthenol for that added moisture. You’ll want to part your hair into sections to apply the product directly to the scalp, she says, and she recommends something like the Kérastase Nutritive Hydrating Scalp Serum; it’s a lightweight leave-in treatment made with plant-based proteins, glycerin, panthenol, and niacinamide to provide targeted hydration. Dr. King likes The Ordinary Natural Moisturizing Factors + HA for Scalp, which she says is packed with moisturizing factors that replicate components naturally found in skin to help keep the skin hydrated.

Conditioning your hair is still an important part of your routine, particularly if you’re experiencing dryness along the hair shaft as well as on your scalp. Dr. Stephens says this is especially important for curly and coily hair textures, which may need more conditioning along the hair shaft even when the scalp itself isn’t dry. She likes the CeraVe Gentle Hydrating Conditioner, which contains known hydrating ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and glycerin to support the skin barrier. “It’s also suitable for all curl patterns, including curly and coily hair, and helps leave the hair feeling softer and more manageable after cleansing,” she says.

Dr. Chang recommends applying conditioner primarily to the midlengths and ends to keep hair hydrated and to reduce breakage. We like the Nécessaire The Conditioner, as it’s fragrance-free and made with nourishing ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid to keep hair hydrated and healthy.

Environmental stressors like the sun’s harmful UV rays can exacerbate dryness, which is why Dr. Chang encourages patients to use proper sun protection, such as hats and scalp-friendly sunscreen (we like the Sun Bum SPF 30 Sunscreen Scalp and Hair Mist Spray or the Coola Scalp Hair Spray Sunscreen SPF 30 Mist) on exposed areas. This is particularly important for anyone with thinning hair or a visible scalp.

Though it can feel soothing, Dr. Chang says to avoid washing your hair in excessively hot water, as it can dry out your scalp. Instead, use lukewarm water and keep your showers short to avoid stripping your scalp of its natural oils.

You’ll also want to avoid excessive product buildup, as heavy oils, dry shampoos, and styling products can accumulate on the scalp and potentially contribute to irritation. Regular cleansing will be key, so use the right water temperature.

Anyone can experience a dry scalp, regardless of skin tone, skin type, or hair texture, Dr. Stephens says. But people with sensitive skin, eczema, or a history of contact dermatitis may be more susceptible. Dr. Chang adds that lifestyle and environmental factors (think cold weather, low humidity, and indoor heating during the winter), as well as age, can play a role.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dry Hair?

Distinguishing between dry scalp and dry hair matters when you’re trying to find the best products to address each concern. “One of the biggest misconceptions I see, particularly among patients with curly and coily hair, is that dry hair automatically means dry scalp,” Dr. Stephens says. “It doesn’t. Tightly coiled hair is more prone to dryness along the hair shaft, partly because natural scalp oils don’t distribute as easily down the curls. But the scalp underneath may be perfectly balanced or even oily. That’s why I encourage people to think of their scalp and hair as two areas with different needs.”

Dr. Chang says to think of it like this: Hair dryness is about how moisture and natural oils travel along the hair shaft, while scalp dryness is more closely related to skin barrier function, sebum production, underlying skin conditions, and environmental exposures.

What Ingredients Should You Avoid to Prevent a Dry Scalp?

Dr. Rabach lists hair dyes, fragrance, and certain alcohols as common culprits that can dry out the scalp and may be worth avoiding. Dr. Stephens agrees and adds that harsh cleansing formulas with alcohol can strip away too much of your scalp’s protective surface (especially when used too frequently) and can be drying or irritating.

Other ingredients to look out for, she says, are essential oils. “They don’t necessarily dry out the scalp directly, but they can trigger irritation or allergic contact dermatitis, which may leave the scalp feeling tight, itchy, or uncomfortable,” she says.

With ingredients like salicylic acid, which help with scalp issues such as dandruff, you still want to be careful, as they may worsen dryness if you use them too often. She adds that just because something is labeled “sulfate-free,” it doesn’t automatically mean it's gentle. You want to consider the formulation as a whole. “It’s important to remember that the overall formulation matters more than any single ingredient,” she says.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dandruff?

Dr. Chang says flaking doesn’t always mean your scalp is dry. Dandruff is generally considered a mild form of seborrheic dermatitis, a condition associated with Malassezia yeast, scalp oils, and inflammation. You’ll need a special type of treatment for these scalp conditions, and it’s best to consult your dermatologist for a proper diagnosis.

Dr. King adds that if you’re experiencing persistent itching, redness, thick scales, crusting, significant flaking, or any pain, it may be time to seek professional help. “I’d recommend evaluation rather than assuming it’s simple dryness,” she says.

First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional insight into the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For scalp moisturizing products, we selected the best based on ingredients, texture, ease of application, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address. #6726. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6725. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6724. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Pair it with the rest of our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

#6720. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6716. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

This section of the Lumina simulation shows the gas temperature in different parts of the early universe, with redder areas showing active galaxy clusters.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.

The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469

#6714. The 9 Most-Wanted Accessories of Fall—and How to Style Them Now

Among all the standout pieces on our fall shopping lists, it was the accessories that emerged as the real heroes. Both the fall and spring collections placed a renewed emphasis on personal style, with accessories offering some of the most compelling ways to make a look your own.

A necklace becomes more personal with the addition of collected charms, while a blazer or knit takes on new character with a brooch pinned to its lapel. Just as important is how these accessories are worn. Consider the strand of pearls layered beneath a sheer knit at The Row, or the silk scarf fastened around the waist like a cummerbund, rather than tied around the neck, at Polo Ralph Lauren. Sometimes, the smallest styling decisions make the biggest impact.

What these accessories have in common, beyond their styling potential, is their desirability. Between the fashion month street style set, our editors' own wish lists and wardrobes, and the collections we've seen since the fall shows, a clear picture has emerged of the accessories everyone wants to wear. Below, we've rounded up the season's most coveted pieces, along with a styling formula for each. From tasseled loafers to sculptural earrings, consider this your guide to the finishing touches that make an outfit.

Never underestimate the styling power of a delicate white floral brooch. Chanel's iconic camellia appeared in both the fall and spring collections, inspiring showgoers throughout fashion month to pin their own floral flourishes onto jackets and coats. The accessory has also become a favorite among Vogue editors (myself included), thanks to its ability to transform even the simplest outerwear. To offset its inherent femininity, try pairing one with a graphic T-shirt and a tailored blazer.

If there was one shoe silhouette that dominated the season, it was the pump. Lace-up iterations from Marni and Prada were particularly covetable, bringing a tougher, more directional attitude to an otherwise ladylike classic. Their appeal extends well beyond the traditionally feminine dresser. Lean into their unconventional proportions with a pair of skirted trousers and a brightly colored knit.

This is one trend I've had particular fun experimenting with, not least because it can be achieved with a simple rectangular silk scarf. Fold it in half lengthwise, wrap it around your waist, and knot it at the back, keeping the front wide and flat. It's a small styling trick that has transformed my trousers and tailoring, lending even a plain white T-shirt a certain polish. For the full effect, take a cue from Polo Ralph Lauren and embrace tuxedo-inspired dressing, right down to the patent leather slip-ons.

Eclectic charm necklaces were everywhere on the fall runways, from Celine and Altuzarra to Dries Van Noten and Marni. But what makes this jewelry trend especially appealing is the opportunity to make it entirely your own. You could, of course, invest in a ready-made version from Celine, but there's something even more charming about collecting medallions, keepsakes, and pendants over time and stringing them together yourself. Let a classic khaki trench and a fluted skirt provide the perfect backdrop.

Of all the re-edition Fendi Baguettes that caught our attention this season, the tiger-print version stood out for its nostalgic appeal. After several seasons of leopard print—and a sprinkling of zebra in the resort collections—tiger stripes offer a fresh alternative within the animal-print family. The trick is to let the print do the talking. Pair a tiger-striped bag with sleek black separates, such as a leather trench, knit dress, and ballet flats.

Call it the Phoebe Philo effect: The oversized statement earring is back, this time in sculptural clusters and explosive, burst-like shapes. What makes these earrings particularly interesting isn't just their scale, but the nonchalance with which they're worn. Rather than saving them for special occasions, consider them a form of everyday extravagance. A pair can do wonders for an otherwise understated combination of white jeans, a leather jacket, and ankle boots.

One reliable measure of an accessory's desirability? How difficult it is to get your hands on one. The Row's Calden tassel loafers have proved particularly elusive, cementing the menswear-inspired silhouette as one of fall's most-wanted shoes. Their appeal lies in their versatility: polished enough for tailoring, yet relaxed enough for everyday wear. A lived-in denim-on-denim look is just one way to put them to work.

At The Row, a simple strand of pearls was worn beneath a sheer, long-sleeved turtleneck rather than over it. The effect was subtle, unexpected, and remarkably chic. It's precisely this kind of styling that has brought the classic pearl necklace back into focus, though there's still plenty to be said for the traditional double-wrapped strand. Look to jewelry favorites Chan Luu and Sophie Buhai, as well as Toteme, for modern interpretations of the heirloom staple. Pearls also played a key styling role in By Malene Birger's lookbooks and on Valentino's runway, further proving their renewed appeal.

Belts have long been an essential finishing touch, but this season, it's the details that deserve a closer look. At Tory Burch's fall show, woven leather belts replaced their smooth counterparts—a seemingly minor distinction that made all the difference. Removed from their usual coastal-prep context, braided belts take on a decidedly more downtown attitude. Try one threaded through a pair of relaxed corduroys, finished with a purple barn jacket for an unexpected pop of color.
